questions.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.x: Washington served two terms from 1789 to 1797 and then voluntarily stepped down, setting a precedent that lasted over a century.

questions.q: Which ancient civilization built the pyramids at Giza?
questions.x: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC and stayed the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years.

questions.q: In which year did World War II end?
questions.x: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August and September, ending a war that involved more than 30 countries.

questions.q: Which famous ocean liner sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
questions.x: The Titanic sank on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York. It carried lifeboats for only about half of the people on board.

questions.q: Which explorer reached the Caribbean in 1492 on a voyage funded by Spain?
questions.x: Columbus was Italian-born and sailed west hoping to reach Asia. He made landfall in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492.

questions.q: Which divided city's wall came down in 1989?
questions.x: The Berlin Wall opened on November 9, 1989. Germany reunified less than a year later, on October 3, 1990.

questions.q: Who became the first emperor of Rome in 27 BC?
questions.x: Born Octavian, he was Julius Caesar's adopted heir. The month of August is named in his honor.

questions.q: Which vast empire was founded by Genghis Khan in the early 1200s?
questions.x: At its height the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.

questions.q: Which French leader crowned himself emperor in 1804?
questions.x: At his coronation in Notre-Dame, Napoleon took the crown from the pope's hands and placed it on his own head.

questions.q: In which year was the American Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.x: Congress approved the final text on July 4, 1776. Most delegates actually signed it about a month later, on August 2.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek city-state was famous for its tough warrior culture?
questions.x: Spartan boys began military training at age seven. Our word "laconic" comes from Laconia, the region around Sparta.

questions.q: Which Egyptian queen joined forces with Mark Antony against Octavian?
questions.x: Cleopatra VII was actually of Greek Macedonian descent and was said to be the first of her dynasty to learn the Egyptian language.

questions.q: Which young pharaoh's nearly intact tomb was found by Howard Carter in 1922?
questions.x: The tomb in the Valley of the Kings held more than 5,000 objects, including a solid gold funeral mask.

questions.q: Who was British Prime Minister for most of World War II?
questions.x: Churchill took office in May 1940. He also won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical and biographical writing.

questions.q: Which dictator led Nazi Germany from 1933 until 1945?
questions.x: Hitler was born in Austria, not Germany. He became chancellor in January 1933 and took his own life in Berlin in April 1945.

questions.q: Which Hawaiian naval base was attacked on December 7, 1941?
questions.x: The surprise attack by Japan led the United States to declare war the next day and enter World War II.

questions.q: Which German monk sparked the Protestant Reformation with his 95 Theses in 1517?
questions.x: The printing press spread Luther's ideas across Europe with astonishing speed, far faster than earlier reform movements.

questions.q: Which battle in 1815 ended Napoleon's rule for good?
questions.x: Napoleon was beaten in present-day Belgium by Wellington and Blucher, then exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena.

questions.q: Which ancient civilization built Machu Picchu high in the Andes?
questions.x: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 as an estate for an Inca emperor and was abandoned about a century later.

questions.q: Which ancient empire built the Colosseum in its capital city?
questions.x: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 and could hold roughly 50,000 spectators, with 80 entrances to speed crowds in and out.

questions.q: Which US president was assassinated in Dallas in 1963?
questions.x: Kennedy was the 35th president and, at age 43 when elected, the youngest person ever chosen for the office.

questions.q: Who was President of the United States during the Civil War?
questions.x: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and is the only president to have held a patent, for a device to lift boats.

questions.q: Which country launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957?
questions.x: Sputnik was about the size of a beach ball. Its radio beeps were heard around the world and kicked off the space race.

questions.q: Who became the first human to travel into space in 1961?
questions.x: Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight on April 12, 1961 lasted just 108 minutes and made one orbit of Earth.

questions.q: Which brothers made the first powered, controlled airplane flights in 1903?
questions.x: Orville's first flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet.

questions.q: Who introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1450?
questions.x: The Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz, was among the first major books produced this way. About 49 copies survive today.

questions.q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon River with his army in 49 BC?
questions.x: The act started a civil war. His reported words "the die is cast" have become a phrase for an irreversible decision.

questions.q: Who became the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in 1979?
questions.x: Thatcher won three general elections in a row and served for 11 years, the longest continuous term of the 20th century.

questions.q: Which English king was forced to seal the Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.x: The charter was sealed at Runnymede by rebellious barons and limited the king's power by putting him under the law.

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador defeated the Aztec Empire in 1521?
questions.x: Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and relied on local allies who resented Aztec rule.

questions.q: Which leader championed nonviolent resistance in India's fight for independence?
questions.x: Gandhi's 240-mile Salt March in 1930 protested the British salt tax and drew worldwide attention.

questions.q: What was the name of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
questions.x: The Mayflower carried about 102 passengers on a voyage of roughly 66 days before landing near Cape Cod.

questions.q: Which devastating plague killed up to a third of Europeans in the 1300s?
questions.x: It spread along trade routes, probably carried by fleas on rats, and returned in waves for centuries.

questions.q: Which French heroine led armies against the English and was nicknamed the Maid of Orleans?
questions.x: She was just a teenager when she helped lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and was later declared a saint.

questions.q: In which present-day US state was the Battle of the Alamo fought in 1836?
questions.x: The phrase "Remember the Alamo" became a rallying cry, and Texas won independence from Mexico weeks later at San Jacinto.

questions.q: Which Roman city was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79?
questions.x: Ash preserved the city so well that archaeologists can still see graffiti, bread loaves and street shops from nearly 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which Norse explorer reached North America around the year 1000?
questions.x: He named the land Vinland. A Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms the Norse reached North America.

questions.q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
questions.x: It began with the Estates-General meeting in May 1789 and ended the absolute monarchy that had ruled France for centuries.

questions.q: Which Paris fortress-prison was stormed by a crowd on July 14, 1789?
questions.x: Only seven prisoners were inside, but the fall of the Bastille became the symbol of the Revolution, and July 14 is now France's national day.

questions.q: Which US president led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II?
questions.x: Roosevelt was elected four times, and the 22nd Amendment was later passed to limit presidents to two terms.

questions.q: At which Washington, D.C. monument did Martin Luther King Jr. give his "I Have a Dream" speech?
questions.x: About 250,000 people gathered for the March on Washington on August 28, 1963. The famous dream passage was partly improvised.

questions.q: Which Venetian merchant-explorer wrote of his travels to the court of Kublai Khan?
questions.x: Marco Polo spent about 24 years away, and his book inspired later explorers, including Columbus, who owned a copy.

questions.q: In which year did World War I begin?
questions.x: The war began in July and August 1914 and lasted four years. It was the first major conflict to use machine guns and tanks on a large scale.

questions.q: Whose assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered World War I?
questions.x: He was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Within about six weeks, a chain of alliances had pulled the major European powers into war.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Inca Empire?
questions.x: Cusco was laid out in the shape of a puma, and many Inca stone walls there fit so tightly that they survived earthquakes.

questions.q: Which British queen reigned from 1837 to 1901?
questions.x: Her 63-year reign, the longest of any British monarch until 2015, gave its name to an entire era.

questions.q: Which English king had six wives?
questions.x: A popular rhyme sums up their fates: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher tutored the young Alexander of Macedon?
questions.x: Aristotle taught Alexander from about age 13, and the king later had scientific specimens sent back to his old teacher.

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer was the first to reach India by sea from Europe, in 1498?
questions.x: His voyage around Africa opened a direct sea route to the spice trade and made Portugal enormously rich.

questions.q: Which US document opens with the words "We the People"?
questions.x: The Constitution was signed in Philadelphia in 1787 and is the oldest written national constitution still in use.

questions.q: Which two Japanese cities were hit by atomic bombs in August 1945?
questions.x: These remain the only two times nuclear weapons have been used in war. Japan announced its surrender days later.

questions.q: Which US president resigned in 1974 because of the Watergate scandal?
questions.x: Nixon is the only US president ever to resign. His successor Gerald Ford had never been elected as president or vice president.

questions.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
questions.x: Armstrong radioed "The Eagle has landed." The command module that stayed in orbit was named Columbia.

questions.q: Who was freed in 1990 after 27 years in prison and became South Africa's president in 1994?
questions.x: Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk and became the first president elected in fully democratic elections.

questions.q: Which empire did Suleiman the Magnificent rule in the 1500s?
questions.x: Suleiman reigned 46 years, expanded his realm into Europe and North Africa, and is also remembered as "the Lawgiver."

questions.q: Which Mesoamerican civilization built the pyramid of Chichen Itza?
questions.x: At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun creates a shadow like a snake slithering down the pyramid's staircase.

questions.q: What was the capital city of the Aztec Empire?
questions.x: Built on an island in a lake, it had causeways and floating gardens. Mexico City now stands on its ruins.

questions.q: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1607?
questions.x: Jamestown in Virginia struggled through disease and hunger at first, but it survived thanks in part to tobacco farming.

questions.q: Which British nurse, known as "the Lady with the Lamp," reformed hospital care during the Crimean War?
questions.x: Nightingale was also a pioneering statistician and invented a type of pie chart to show how many soldiers died from preventable disease.

questions.q: Who received the first US patent for the telephone in 1876?
questions.x: Bell's assistant Thomas Watson heard the first telephone words: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."

questions.q: Which revolutionary led the Bolsheviks to power in Russia in 1917?
questions.x: Lenin returned to Russia from exile in Switzerland in a sealed train, arriving in Petrograd in April 1917.

questions.q: Which two superpowers were the main rivals in the Cold War?
a: The United States and the Soviet Union
questions.x: They never fought each other directly, but competed through arms races, the space race and proxy wars from about 1947 to 1991.

questions.q: Which US president arranged the Louisiana Purchase in 1803?
questions.x: The purchase from France cost about 15 million dollars and roughly doubled the size of the United States.

questions.q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World stood on the island of Pharos near Alexandria?
questions.x: Built in the 3rd century BC, it was possibly over 100 meters tall and the word for lighthouse in several languages comes from Pharos.

questions.q: Which French king was known as the Sun King?
questions.x: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years, the longest of any major European monarch, and built the Palace of Versailles.

questions.q: Which country did Germany invade on September 1, 1939, starting World War II in Europe?
questions.x: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on September 3.

questions.q: On D-Day in June 1944, Allied troops landed on the beaches of which region of France?
questions.x: Over 150,000 troops crossed the English Channel on the first day in the largest seaborne invasion in history.

questions.q: Which leader proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949?
questions.x: Mao announced the new state from Tiananmen Gate in Beijing on October 1, 1949.

questions.q: Who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1932?
questions.x: Earhart disappeared in 1937 over the Pacific while attempting to fly around the world, and her fate remains a mystery.

questions.q: Who made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic in 1927?
questions.x: Lindbergh flew the "Spirit of St. Louis" from New York to Paris in about 33.5 hours and won a 25,000-dollar prize.

questions.q: Whose refusal to give up her bus seat in 1955 helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott?
questions.x: The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

questions.q: Which woman helped many enslaved people escape north on the Underground Railroad?
questions.x: Tubman escaped slavery herself in 1849 and made about 13 trips back to the South, reportedly never losing a passenger.

questions.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the early 1500s?
questions.x: Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor and reportedly resisted the commission, which took about four years.

questions.q: In which year did the Great Fire of London occur?
questions.x: The fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane and destroyed about 13,000 houses, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded.

questions.q: What name is given to the ancient Egyptian system of picture writing?
questions.x: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, helped scholars finally decipher hieroglyphs after about 1,400 years of silence.

questions.q: Which English queen saw her navy defeat the Spanish Armada in 1588?
questions.x: Elizabeth rallied troops at Tilbury saying she had "the heart and stomach of a king." Storms also helped wreck the Spanish fleet.

questions.q: What was the 1773 protest in which colonists threw tea into Boston Harbor called?
questions.x: Colonists dumped 342 chests of tea to protest taxation without representation, which pushed Britain toward harsher laws and then revolution.

questions.q: In dating years, what do the letters BC stand for?
questions.x: The system was devised by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus around AD 525. There is no year zero between 1 BC and AD 1.

questions.q: Which Italian dictator was known as "Il Duce"?
questions.x: Mussolini founded the Fascist movement and ruled Italy from 1922 until 1943, when the Allied invasion of Sicily led to his removal.

questions.q: In which Dutch city did Anne Frank and her family hide during World War II?
questions.x: The family hid for over two years in a concealed annex above her father's business. Her diary has been translated into over 60 languages.

questions.q: Which event in October 1929 helped trigger the Great Depression?
a: The Wall Street stock market crash
questions.x: Stock prices collapsed over several days around "Black Tuesday," October 29, and the Dow Jones average did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954.

questions.q: Which American scientist developed the first successful polio vaccine in the 1950s?
questions.x: Salk refused to patent the vaccine. When asked who owned it, he reportedly said, "Could you patent the sun?"

questions.q: Which Italian astronomer was tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for supporting a Sun-centered universe?
questions.x: Galileo spent his last years under house arrest, yet his telescope observations of Jupiter's moons transformed astronomy.

questions.q: From which region of Europe did the Vikings come?
questions.x: Vikings from today's Norway, Sweden and Denmark raided and traded from about AD 793 to 1066, reaching Russia, Iceland and North America.

questions.q: Which canal, opened in 1914, linked the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
questions.x: Ships crossing it are raised by locks about 26 meters above sea level, saving a journey of thousands of miles around South America.

questions.q: What animals did the Carthaginian general Hannibal famously bring across the Alps to attack Rome?
questions.x: He crossed in 218 BC with a force that included dozens of elephants, though most of them died from the cold and the harsh journey.

questions.q: Ancient Egyptian civilization grew up along the banks of which river?
questions.x: Yearly floods left fertile black silt, and the Egyptians called their land Kemet, meaning "the black land."

questions.q: Which Greek city-state is credited with inventing democracy?
questions.x: Athenian democracy began around 508 BC, but only free adult male citizens could vote, and women and enslaved people were excluded.

questions.q: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
questions.x: Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 and the Romanov dynasty, which had ruled since 1613, came to an end.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek poet is credited with composing the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.x: The epics were passed down orally before being written, and the Iliad tells of the final weeks of the Trojan War.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
questions.x: The city, founded by Emperor Constantine in AD 330, is now called Istanbul and sits on two continents.

questions.q: Edward Jenner's pioneering vaccine helped humanity eventually wipe out which disease?
questions.x: Jenner tested his idea in 1796 using cowpox. Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980.

questions.q: Which American businessman introduced the moving assembly line for cars in 1913?
questions.x: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes, making cars affordable.

questions.q: Who assassinated President Abraham Lincoln in 1865?
questions.x: Booth was an actor, and the shooting took place at Ford's Theatre in Washington days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox.

questions.q: Which US space shuttle broke apart shortly after launch in January 1986?
questions.x: The accident, caused by a failed rubber seal in cold weather, led to a 32-month pause in shuttle flights.

questions.q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.x: The Games were revived by Frenchman Pierre de Coubertin. About 14 nations took part, and the marathon was added in memory of a legendary Greek runner.

questions.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin in the 1700s?
questions.x: Britain had coal, iron, capital and colonial markets, and its textile mills and steam engines became models for the world.

questions.q: Which scientist became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, in 1903?
questions.x: Curie won in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911, becoming the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

questions.q: Which ship sank on its maiden voyage in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
questions.x: The Titanic sank in the North Atlantic with more than 1,500 people lost.

questions.q: Which queen of Egypt was linked with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
questions.x: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt.

questions.q: In which year did the Western Roman Empire traditionally fall?
questions.x: In 476 the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Roman Empire lasted almost another thousand years.

questions.q: Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BC?
questions.x: Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The Cyrus Cylinder from that time is often described as an early statement on tolerance of subject peoples.

questions.q: From which North African city did the general Hannibal come?
questions.x: Carthage lay near modern Tunis. Rome fought three Punic Wars against it and finally destroyed the city in 146 BC.

questions.q: William of Normandy defeated which Anglo-Saxon king at Hastings in 1066?
questions.x: Harold had marched his army about 250 miles in under three weeks after beating a Norwegian invasion in the north.

questions.q: Alexander the Great was king of which kingdom?
questions.x: Alexander took the throne at age 20 and created an empire reaching from Greece to northwestern India before dying at 32.

questions.q: Which Spartan king led the Greek defense at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
questions.x: Leonidas and his 300 Spartans, with several thousand allies, held a narrow pass against the huge Persian army for three days.

questions.q: Who unified China in 221 BC and became its first emperor?
questions.x: He standardized writing, money and measurements, and linked earlier defensive walls that became the first Great Wall.

questions.q: Near which Chinese city was the Terracotta Army discovered in 1974?
questions.x: Farmers digging a well found the army, which includes more than 8,000 life-size soldiers, each with a different face.

questions.q: Mansa Musa, famed for his wealth and a 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, ruled which empire?
questions.x: He gave away so much gold in Cairo that the price of gold there reportedly stayed depressed for years.

questions.q: In which year did the Suez Canal open?
questions.x: The canal linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea cut thousands of miles off voyages between Europe and Asia.

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer led the 1519 expedition that became the first to sail around the world?
questions.x: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Only 18 men of about 270 completed the voyage, under Juan Sebastian Elcano.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor issued the Edict of Milan in 313, tolerating Christianity?
questions.x: Constantine also moved the capital east, founding Constantinople in AD 330 on the site of the old city of Byzantium.

questions.q: Which Scottish queen was executed in 1587 on the orders of Elizabeth I?
questions.x: Mary had been held in English captivity for nearly 19 years. Her son James VI later inherited Elizabeth's throne.

questions.q: In which year did the English defeat the Spanish Armada?
questions.x: The English used fireships to scatter the Spanish fleet at Gravelines, and storms on the long route home destroyed many more ships.

questions.q: Which 1648 settlement ended the Thirty Years' War?
questions.x: Westphalia is often seen as the start of the modern system of sovereign states, and the war had devastated much of Germany.

questions.q: Which French king was executed during the Revolution in January 1793?
questions.x: Louis XVI had been king since 1774. His wife Marie Antoinette was executed nine months later.

questions.q: To which Mediterranean island was Napoleon first exiled in 1814?
questions.x: Napoleon escaped from Elba in February 1815 and returned to power for the Hundred Days, which ended at Waterloo.

questions.q: Which British admiral won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed in the fighting?
questions.x: Nelson's signal "England expects that every man will do his duty" is still famous. The victory ended Napoleon's hopes of invading Britain.

questions.q: Which Prussian statesman engineered the unification of Germany in 1871?
questions.x: Bismarck used three short wars against Denmark, Austria and France to build the German Empire, which was proclaimed at Versailles.

questions.q: Which Italian patriot led the Red Shirts in the 1860 campaign to unify Italy?
questions.x: Garibaldi conquered Sicily and Naples with about a thousand volunteers and then handed his gains to the king of Piedmont.

questions.q: The Charge of the Light Brigade took place during which war?
questions.x: The charge at Balaclava in 1854 resulted from a misunderstood order. Tennyson's poem made it a lasting symbol of courage.

questions.q: Which island was ceded to Britain in 1842 after the First Opium War?
questions.x: The Treaty of Nanking gave Britain Hong Kong Island, which stayed British until 1997, along with the opening of five Chinese ports to trade.

questions.q: Which event of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and returned power to the Japanese emperor?
questions.x: Japan then modernized at remarkable speed, building railways, a modern army and an industrial economy within a few decades.

questions.q: Which US naval officer's 1853 arrival in Tokyo Bay pressured Japan to open to trade?
questions.x: Perry's "black ships" were steam-powered, which astonished the Japanese. He returned in 1854 and signed a treaty.

questions.q: In 1857 soldiers called sepoys rebelled in India against the rule of which company?
questions.x: After the rebellion, Britain dissolved the company and began ruling India directly under the Crown in 1858.

questions.q: What was the late-1800s race by European powers to claim African territory called?
questions.x: By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 set ground rules among the colonial powers.

questions.q: At which naval battle in 31 BC did Octavian win the war that made him sole ruler of Rome?
questions.x: The victory off western Greece led to Octavian becoming Augustus, and Egypt then became a Roman province.

questions.q: Which Persian king invaded Greece in 480 BC with a vast army and fleet?
questions.x: Xerxes reportedly had a bridge of boats built across the Hellespont. His army burned Athens but his fleet lost at Salamis.

questions.q: Which statesman led Athens during its golden age and oversaw the building of the Parthenon?
questions.x: Pericles guided Athens for about 30 years until a plague killed him in 429 BC during the Peloponnesian War.

questions.q: Which philosopher, a student of Socrates, founded the Academy in Athens?
questions.x: Plato's Academy, founded around 387 BC, operated for centuries and is often called the first university in the Western world.

questions.q: Which French scholar deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822?
questions.x: Champollion used the Rosetta Stone, which carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and realized the signs recorded sounds.

questions.q: Which female pharaoh built a famous mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari?
questions.x: Hatshepsut ruled for about two decades in the 15th century BC and sent a famous trading expedition to the land of Punt.

questions.q: Which pharaoh had the great temples of Abu Simbel carved into a cliff?
questions.x: In the 1960s the temples were cut apart and moved uphill to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

questions.q: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built?
questions.x: Khufu's pyramid held about 2.3 million stone blocks. The Greeks later called him Cheops.

questions.q: Which Babylonian king issued a famous law code around 1750 BC?
questions.x: The code was carved on a tall black stone slab, now in the Louvre, and includes the principle of "an eye for an eye."

questions.q: Which people of ancient Mesopotamia developed cuneiform writing?
questions.x: Cuneiform began around 3400 BC as pictures pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus, originally to keep trade records.

questions.q: Which grandson of Genghis Khan founded China's Yuan dynasty?
questions.x: Kublai completed the conquest of Song China in 1279 and moved his capital to what is now Beijing.

questions.q: Which Chinese admiral led giant treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?
questions.x: His voyages reached East Africa and were larger than any European fleet of the time, but China halted them after his death.

questions.q: In which year did the Ottomans capture Constantinople?
questions.x: Sultan Mehmed II was just 21. The Ottomans used enormous cannons to breach the city's ancient walls, ending the Byzantine Empire.

questions.q: Which English king won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
questions.x: English longbowmen helped Henry's much smaller army defeat the French on a muddy field during the Hundred Years' War.

questions.q: Which English king was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485?
questions.x: His death ended the Wars of the Roses and began the Tudor dynasty. His skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester in 2012.

questions.q: Which 1534 act made the English monarch head of the Church of England?
questions.x: Henry VIII pushed it through after the pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

questions.q: Which Polish astronomer proposed a Sun-centered model of the universe in 1543?
questions.x: His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was published as he lay near death in 1543.

questions.q: Which conquistador captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532?
questions.x: Pizarro's small force of fewer than 200 men took the emperor prisoner at Cajamarca and then collected a huge ransom of gold.

questions.q: Columbus's 1492 fleet consisted of the Santa Maria, the Pinta and which other ship?
questions.x: The Santa Maria ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day 1492, and its timbers were used to build a fort.

questions.q: On which ship did Francis Drake sail around the world between 1577 and 1580?
questions.x: Drake returned laden with Spanish treasure and was knighted aboard his ship by Elizabeth I in 1581.

questions.q: Which British navigator charted the east coast of Australia in 1770?
questions.x: Cook's ship Endeavour was nearly lost on the Great Barrier Reef, and he claimed the coast for Britain as New South Wales.

questions.q: Which Scottish missionary-explorer was famously found by Henry Morton Stanley in 1871?
questions.x: Stanley is said to have greeted him with "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?" Livingstone had not been heard from in years.

questions.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
questions.x: Amundsen's Norwegian team used sled dogs and beat Scott's British party by about five weeks.

questions.q: Which Shoshone woman guided the Lewis and Clark expedition?
questions.x: She joined the journey while carrying her infant son. Her presence helped signal peaceful intentions to other nations.

questions.q: The 1848 discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill set off a rush to which region?
questions.x: By 1849 tens of thousands of "forty-niners" had poured in, and San Francisco grew from a village into a major city.

questions.q: In which state was the Battle of Gettysburg fought in July 1863?
questions.x: The three-day battle was the bloodiest of the Civil War. Lincoln spoke at the cemetery four months later.

questions.q: In which year did Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
questions.x: It took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in Confederate-held territory free. The 13th Amendment ended slavery nationwide in 1865.

questions.q: In which US state did the first transcontinental railroad join up at Promontory Summit in 1869?
questions.x: A ceremonial golden spike marked the meeting of the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines, cutting cross-country travel from months to days.

questions.q: In which year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
questions.x: It was signed on June 28, 1919, exactly five years after the assassination in Sarajevo, and required Germany to pay reparations.

questions.q: In which year was the Battle of the Somme fought?
questions.x: On the first day, July 1, 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties, its worst single day.

questions.q: Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German U-boat in 1915?
questions.x: The sinking off Ireland killed nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans, and turned US public opinion against Germany.

questions.q: Who founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923?
questions.x: The surname Ataturk, meaning "father of the Turks," was given to him in 1934. He also replaced the Arabic script with a Latin-based alphabet.

questions.q: In which year did India gain independence from Britain?
questions.x: At independence in August 1947 the subcontinent was divided into India and Pakistan, in one of history's largest migrations.

questions.q: Which general led the Nationalist side to victory in the Spanish Civil War?
questions.x: The war lasted from 1936 to 1939, and Franco ruled Spain until his death in 1975.

questions.q: Which city's 1942-43 battle ended with the surrender of Germany's 6th Army?
questions.x: The battle is often called the turning point on the Eastern Front. The city is now called Volgograd.

questions.q: From which French port were over 330,000 Allied troops evacuated in May and June 1940?
questions.x: Hundreds of small civilian boats joined navy ships in the rescue, which Churchill called "a miracle of deliverance."

questions.q: What was the code name of the US project that built the first atomic bombs?
questions.x: The project employed over 100,000 people, with major sites at Los Alamos, Oak Ridge and Hanford, and the first test came in July 1945.

questions.q: In which German city were leading Nazis tried after World War II?
questions.x: The Nuremberg trials began in November 1945 and helped set precedents for international law on war crimes.

questions.q: Which US Secretary of State gave his name to the 1948 plan to rebuild Western Europe?
questions.x: The plan sent about 13 billion dollars in aid, and Marshall received the 1953 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.q: In which year was NATO founded?
questions.x: Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington in April 1949, promising to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

questions.q: Which line of latitude divided Korea into two zones in 1945?
questions.x: Two young US officers chose the line in a matter of minutes using a National Geographic map.

questions.q: Which Soviet leader agreed to withdraw missiles from Cuba in 1962?
questions.x: The 13-day standoff ended when the US secretly agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey and pledged not to invade Cuba.

questions.q: Who became the first woman in space in 1963?
questions.x: Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times in Vostok 6. The next woman in space did not follow until 1982.

questions.q: Who became the first American in space in May 1961?
questions.x: Shepard's suborbital flight lasted only about 15 minutes. Ten years later he walked on the Moon on Apollo 14.

questions.q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
questions.x: East Germany put up barbed wire and then concrete overnight on August 13, 1961 to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West.

questions.q: In which year was the Soviet Union dissolved?
questions.x: It ended on December 26, 1991, after Mikhail Gorbachev resigned and fifteen republics became independent countries.

questions.q: Which Scottish engineer greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s?
questions.x: The unit of power, the watt, is named after him. He also introduced the term "horsepower."

questions.q: Which English engineer built the locomotive Rocket, which won a famous trial in 1829?
questions.x: Rocket reached about 30 miles per hour and helped prove steam locomotives could run passenger railways.

questions.q: Who invented the cotton gin in 1793?
questions.x: The machine made cleaning cotton far faster, which dramatically expanded cotton farming and, tragically, slavery in the American South.

questions.q: Which American developed the electric telegraph and a code of dots and dashes?
questions.x: The first official message, sent in 1844 from Washington to Baltimore, was "What hath God wrought."

questions.q: On which ship did Charles Darwin sail around the world from 1831 to 1836?
questions.x: The voyage took Darwin to the Galapagos Islands, where his observations of finches helped shape his theory of evolution.

questions.q: Which British MP led the long campaign that ended the slave trade in the British Empire in 1807?
questions.x: Wilberforce lived to hear that the Slavery Abolition Act, which freed slaves across the empire, was passing in 1833.

questions.q: Who led the Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791?
questions.x: Haiti became independent in 1804 and was the first republic led by formerly enslaved people.

questions.q: Which Venezuelan-born leader helped liberate Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain?
questions.x: Bolivia is named in his honor, and he was often called El Libertador.

questions.q: Which Zulu king built a powerful military state in southern Africa in the early 1800s?
questions.x: Shaka reorganized his army, introducing a short stabbing spear and the "buffalo horns" formation.

questions.q: Which African country defeated an Italian invasion force at the Battle of Adwa in 1896?
questions.x: Emperor Menelik II's victory kept Ethiopia independent and made it a symbol of resistance to colonialism.

questions.q: The 1911 revolution in China ended the rule of which dynasty?
questions.x: The last emperor, Puyi, was a child of six. The Qing had ruled since 1644, and the Republic of China was proclaimed in 1912.

questions.q: William the Conqueror ordered which great survey of England, completed in 1086?
questions.x: The survey recorded who owned land, livestock and mills in nearly every English village, and gave the king a detailed picture of his wealth.

questions.q: Which Frankish king was crowned Emperor by the pope on Christmas Day in 800?
questions.x: Charlemagne ruled much of Western Europe and promoted learning, helping spark a revival now called the Carolingian Renaissance.

questions.q: Which Russian tsar founded the city of St. Petersburg in 1703?
questions.x: Peter built it on marshland as a "window to the West," and it served as Russia's capital for over 200 years.

questions.q: At which Virginia town did British General Cornwallis surrender in 1781?
questions.x: A French fleet trapped Cornwallis from the sea while Washington's and Rochambeau's armies surrounded him by land.

questions.q: In 1814, British troops burned public buildings in which American city?
questions.x: The burning of the White House and Capitol happened during the War of 1812. A rainstorm helped put out the fires.

questions.q: In which year did the 19th Amendment guarantee American women the right to vote?
questions.x: The amendment was ratified in August 1920 after about 72 years of campaigning that began at the Seneca Falls convention in 1848.

questions.q: Which British suffragette leader founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903?
questions.x: The group's motto was "Deeds, not words." British women over 30 gained the vote in 1918, a decade before full equality.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
questions.x: Construction took about 20 years from the 1630s, and the white marble mausoleum is said to have involved some 20,000 workers.

questions.q: Mesopotamia, the cradle of early civilization, lay between the Tigris and which other river?
questions.x: The name Mesopotamia means "between the rivers" in Greek, and the region included the first cities such as Ur and Uruk.

questions.q: Which Chinese dynasty followed the short-lived Qin and ruled for about four centuries?
questions.x: Under the Han, the Silk Road opened and paper was invented. The majority ethnic group of China still calls itself "Han."

questions.q: In which year did the Gunpowder Plot to blow up the English Parliament take place?
questions.x: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath the House of Lords, and Britons still mark Bonfire Night each November 5.

questions.q: Which Chinese dynasty built the Forbidden City in Beijing in the early 1400s?
questions.x: Construction began in 1406 under the Yongle Emperor. The palace complex has nearly 1,000 buildings and housed 24 emperors.

questions.q: Which US president signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
questions.x: Johnson signed it on July 2, 1964, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

questions.q: Who was Emperor of Japan during World War II?
questions.x: Hirohito reigned from 1926 to 1989, the longest of any Japanese emperor, and his radio address announced Japan's surrender in 1945.

questions.q: Who became India's first female Prime Minister, in 1966?
questions.x: She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, and she served until 1977 and again from 1980 to 1984.

questions.q: Which Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with elephants?
questions.x: Hannibal marched into Italy in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.

questions.q: Which treaty formally ended World War I with Germany in 1919?
questions.x: The treaty was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.

questions.q: In which year BC did the Athenians defeat the Persians at the Battle of Marathon?
questions.x: Legend says a messenger ran about 25 miles to Athens with news of victory, which inspired the modern marathon race.

questions.q: Which 1494 treaty divided newly found lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal?
questions.x: The line ran west of the Cape Verde Islands, which is why Brazil ended up Portuguese-speaking while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

questions.q: At which 1571 naval battle did a Holy League fleet defeat the Ottoman navy?
questions.x: The clash off western Greece was among the largest galley battles ever fought. Miguel de Cervantes was wounded in it.

questions.q: Which Polish king led the relief army that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683?
questions.x: Sobieski led what is considered one of history's largest cavalry charges, and the defeat marked the start of Ottoman decline in central Europe.

questions.q: Which East India Company commander won the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
questions.x: Clive's force was far smaller than the Bengal army, but secret deals with its commanders helped decide the outcome.

questions.q: In which year did Napoleon win the Battle of Austerlitz, his famous "Battle of the Three Emperors"?
questions.x: He defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army on the first anniversary of his coronation, December 2, 1805.

questions.q: In which year did Napoleon launch his invasion of Russia?
questions.x: He crossed the Niemen River with perhaps 450,000 men in June. Only a small fraction survived the retreat that winter.

questions.q: Which 1840 treaty was signed between the British Crown and Maori chiefs in New Zealand?
questions.x: The treaty has English and Maori versions that differ in meaning, which has been the subject of debate and legal claims ever since.

questions.q: Who led the Taiping Rebellion in China from 1850 to 1864?
questions.x: Hong claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus. The rebellion is one of the deadliest civil wars in history, with tens of millions dead.

questions.q: Which US cavalry commander was killed at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876?
questions.x: Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors under leaders including Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse won a rare, decisive victory over the 7th Cavalry.

questions.q: The explosion of which US battleship in Havana harbor in 1898 helped spark the Spanish-American War?
questions.x: "Remember the Maine" became a popular slogan. A later investigation concluded the cause was probably an internal fire rather than an enemy attack.

questions.q: In which US city was the 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War signed?
questions.x: President Theodore Roosevelt mediated the talks and won the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for the effort.

questions.q: The 1915 Gallipoli campaign was an Allied attempt to force which strait?
questions.x: The campaign failed after eight months. It became a founding moment for the national identities of Australia and New Zealand.

questions.q: Which 1918 treaty took Soviet Russia out of World War I?
questions.x: Russia gave up huge territories, including Ukraine and the Baltic states, but Germany's own defeat later in 1918 voided the treaty.

questions.q: In which French forest was the armistice ending World War I signed in November 1918?
questions.x: The signing took place in a railway carriage. In 1940 Hitler made France sign its surrender in the very same carriage.

questions.q: In which city did Hitler lead the failed Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923?
questions.x: The coup attempt failed within a day. Hitler wrote Mein Kampf during the months he spent in prison afterward.

questions.q: The 1938 Munich Agreement forced which country to hand the Sudetenland to Germany?
questions.x: Czechoslovakia was not invited to the conference. Neville Chamberlain returned to Britain promising "peace for our time."

questions.q: What was the code name of Germany's 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union?
questions.x: Launched on June 22, 1941, it involved over three million Axis troops along a front of roughly 1,800 miles.

questions.q: Near which Pacific atoll did the US Navy win a decisive battle in June 1942?
questions.x: US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers, and Japan never regained the initiative in the Pacific.

questions.q: In February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at which Crimean resort?
questions.x: The "Big Three" discussed the postwar order, including the division of Germany and the creation of the United Nations.

questions.q: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
questions.x: Britain, France and Israel invaded in response, but US and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.

questions.q: What was the name of the dog sent into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957?
questions.x: Laika was a stray found on the streets of Moscow. The craft was not designed to return, and she was the first animal to orbit Earth.

questions.q: In 1975, the US Apollo spacecraft docked in orbit with which Soviet craft?
questions.x: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project was a symbol of détente, and the crews shared meals and exchanged gifts in space.

questions.q: Which Soviet space station was launched in 1986 and orbited until 2001?
questions.x: Mir means "peace" or "world" in Russian. It was assembled in orbit over a decade and hosted more than 100 astronauts.

questions.q: Which ruler founded the Akkadian Empire around 2300 BC, creating one of the first empires?
questions.x: Sargon is said to have been born to humble parents and set adrift on a river in a basket, a story later echoed in other legends.

questions.q: Which Assyrian king assembled a great library of clay tablets at Nineveh?
questions.x: His library held tens of thousands of tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, and was rediscovered in the 1850s.

questions.q: Ramses II fought the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BC against which empire?
questions.x: The battle led to the first known peace treaty between two great powers, copies of which survive in both Egyptian and Hittite.

questions.q: Which Mediterranean island was the center of the Minoan civilization?
questions.x: The Minoans built the palace at Knossos, and the myth of the labyrinth and the Minotaur may echo its maze-like layout.

questions.q: Which British archaeologist began excavating the palace of Knossos in 1900?
questions.x: Evans coined the name "Minoan" after the legendary King Minos, and his partial reconstructions of the site remain controversial.

questions.q: Which German amateur archaeologist excavated the site of Troy at Hisarlik in the 1870s?
questions.x: Schliemann dug so quickly and roughly that he probably destroyed layers belonging to the Trojan War era.

questions.q: Which early Mesoamerican civilization is famous for carving colossal stone heads?
questions.x: The Olmec flourished on Mexico's Gulf Coast from about 1200 BC, and some of their heads weigh over 20 tons.

questions.q: Which ruler transformed Cusco into the center of the Inca Empire in the mid-1400s?
questions.x: His name means "he who transforms the earth." He is credited with building Machu Picchu as a royal estate.

questions.q: The ancient Mississippian city of Cahokia lies across the river from which modern US city?
questions.x: Around AD 1100 Cahokia may have had 10,000 to 20,000 people, and its Monks Mound is the largest earthen structure in North America.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor, grandson of Babur, ruled from 1556 to 1605?
questions.x: Akbar was famous for religious tolerance and for hosting scholars of many faiths at his court.

questions.q: Which ruler founded the Mughal Empire after winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
questions.x: Babur descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, and he used gunpowder weapons to defeat a much larger army.

questions.q: Which Mauryan emperor, after the bloody Kalinga war, spread his edicts on stone pillars across India?
questions.x: Ashoka's lion capital from Sarnath is now the national emblem of India, and his pillars are among the oldest surviving Indian inscriptions.

questions.q: Which Khmer king built the temple of Angkor Wat in the 12th century?
questions.x: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world and appears on the flag of Cambodia.

questions.q: Great Zimbabwe, a medieval stone city in southern Africa, was built by ancestors of which people?
questions.x: The site grew rich on gold and cattle between about 1100 and 1450. Modern Zimbabwe takes its name from the ruins.

questions.q: Which Phoenician city is traditionally credited with founding Carthage?
questions.x: Tradition dates the founding to 814 BC and credits Queen Dido, who according to legend outwitted a local ruler to gain land.

questions.q: At which battle in 202 BC did Scipio Africanus defeat Hannibal?
questions.x: The victory ended the Second Punic War and made Rome the dominant power of the western Mediterranean.

questions.q: Who led the great slave revolt against Rome that began in 73 BC?
questions.x: The revolt began with about 70 gladiators escaping from a school in Capua and grew to tens of thousands of followers.

questions.q: Which queen of the Iceni led an uprising against Roman rule in Britain around AD 60?
questions.x: Her forces burned Londinium, Verulamium and Camulodunum before being defeated. A statue of her stands by Westminster Bridge in London.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor divided the empire's rule among four co-rulers in AD 293?
questions.x: The system, called the Tetrarchy, was meant to make the huge empire easier to defend. Diocletian later retired to grow cabbages.

questions.q: Which Germanic leader destroyed three Roman legions at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9?
questions.x: The defeat convinced Emperor Augustus to stop expanding east of the Rhine. He is said to have cried out for his lost legions.

questions.q: Which Visigothic king sacked the city of Rome in AD 410?
questions.x: It was the first time in about 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy, and it shocked the Roman world.

questions.q: Which Byzantine emperor oversaw the building of the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537?
questions.x: The great church was built in under six years and, for nearly a thousand years, was the largest cathedral in the world.

questions.q: Who commanded the Frankish forces at the Battle of Tours in 732?
questions.x: Charles Martel was the grandfather of Charlemagne, and his name means "Charles the Hammer."

questions.q: To which Italian city did the Western Roman emperors move their capital in AD 402?
questions.x: Ravenna's marshes made it easier to defend than Milan, and it later housed splendid mosaics from the Byzantine period.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor wrote the philosophical work Meditations?
questions.x: He wrote it as private notes while on military campaigns. It is regarded as a classic of Stoic philosophy.

questions.q: Which city did Caliph al-Mansur found in 762 as the Abbasid capital?
questions.x: Baghdad's round design earned it the nickname "Round City." It became a center of learning with the House of Wisdom.

questions.q: The word "algorithm" comes from the name of which 9th-century Persian scholar?
questions.x: His book on calculation also gave us the word "algebra," from the Arabic al-jabr.

questions.q: Which king of Wessex defeated the Danes at the Battle of Edington in 878?
questions.x: Alfred is the only English monarch called "the Great" and is credited with founding the English navy and promoting literacy.

questions.q: Which Danish king ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the early 1000s?
questions.x: A story says Cnut sat by the sea and ordered the tide to stop, to show his courtiers that even a king has limits.

questions.q: At which September 1066 battle did an English army beat a Norwegian invasion?
questions.x: The English victory in Yorkshire came just three weeks before the Norman landing in the south.

questions.q: In 1347, plague-bearing ships first reached Europe at which Sicilian port?
questions.x: Genoese trading ships fleeing the Black Sea carried the disease. By 1351 it had swept across nearly all of Europe.

questions.q: Who led the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
questions.x: The rebels marched on London after a poll tax was imposed. Tyler was killed during talks with the young King Richard II.

questions.q: Which Parliamentarian became Lord Protector of England in 1653?
questions.x: After the execution of Charles I, England was a republic. Cromwell refused the crown but held near-royal powers until 1658.

questions.q: Which Dutch prince became King of England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
questions.x: William ruled jointly with his wife Mary II, and the revolution was largely bloodless in England, which is why it is called "Glorious."

questions.q: At the 1709 Battle of Poltava, Peter the Great's Russia decisively defeated which country?
questions.x: The victory over Charles XII ended Sweden's days as a great power and made Russia the leading force in northern Europe.

questions.q: Which Habsburg ruler governed Austria, Hungary and Bohemia from 1740 to 1780?
questions.x: She had 16 children, and her youngest daughter, Marie Antoinette, became Queen of France.

questions.q: Which Jacobin leader dominated the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror?
questions.x: Robespierre himself was overthrown in July 1794, ending the Terror, which had claimed thousands of lives.

questions.q: For which event was the Eiffel Tower built in 1889?
questions.x: The fair marked the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution, and the tower was meant to be dismantled after 20 years.

questions.q: In which year was the Great Exhibition held in London's Crystal Palace?
questions.x: Prince Albert helped organize it. Over six million visits were made, and its profits helped fund London's great museums.

questions.q: Who made the first airplane flight across the English Channel in 1909?
questions.x: Bleriot's flight took about 36 minutes and earned a prize of 1,000 pounds from a British newspaper.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.x: Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a forgotten culture dish. Florey and Chain later turned it into a usable drug.

questions.q: In which US state did the airship Hindenburg burst into flames in 1937?
questions.x: The disaster at Lakehurst, filmed and broadcast on radio, ended the era of passenger airships. Most people aboard survived.

questions.q: Who led Czechoslovakia's reform movement known as the Prague Spring in 1968?
questions.x: Dubcek promoted "socialism with a human face." Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August 1968 to end the reforms.

questions.q: In which year were the Voyager 1 and 2 space probes launched?
questions.x: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and is the most distant human-made object, carrying a golden record of Earth's sounds.

questions.q: Which Athenian lawgiver's reforms around 594 BC laid groundwork for democracy by cancelling debts?
questions.x: Solon freed Athenians who had been enslaved for debt. His rival Draco, by contrast, gave us the word "draconian."

questions.q: What was the name of Alexander the Great's famous horse?
questions.x: Alexander tamed the horse as a boy by turning it toward the sun, since it was frightened of its own shadow.

questions.q: Which Persian king did Alexander defeat at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC?
questions.x: Darius fled the field and was killed by his own officers soon after, leaving Alexander master of the Persian Empire.

questions.q: Which dynasty, founded by a general of Alexander the Great, ruled Egypt until Cleopatra?
questions.x: Ptolemy I founded the Library of Alexandria. Cleopatra VII was the last of the line and the only one said to speak Egyptian.

questions.q: Which calendar did Julius Caesar introduce in 45 BC?
questions.x: It had 365 days and a leap day every four years. It was off by a few minutes a year, and by 1582 the error had reached about ten days.

questions.q: Which pope introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582?
questions.x: To fix the drift, ten days were skipped. In Catholic countries October 4 was followed by October 15, 1582.

questions.q: Which Moroccan traveler journeyed across much of the Old World in the 1300s?
questions.x: He traveled about 75,000 miles over nearly 30 years, visiting places from West Africa to China.

questions.q: Which Portuguese prince sponsored voyages down Africa's coast in the early 1400s?
questions.x: Henry never sailed far himself. He supported navigation research and ships that paved the way for later explorers.

questions.q: Which Portuguese navigator was the first European to round the southern tip of Africa, in 1488?
questions.x: Dias named it the Cape of Storms. King John II renamed it the Cape of Good Hope to inspire hope for a route to India.

questions.q: Which Portuguese navigator reached Brazil in 1500?
questions.x: Cabral was heading for India with a large fleet when his ships were blown far west and he claimed the land for Portugal.

questions.q: Whose first name inspired the naming of the Americas?
questions.x: Mapmaker Martin Waldseemuller used the name America on his 1507 world map after Vespucci argued the lands were a new continent.

questions.q: Which French explorer sailed up the St. Lawrence River in 1534 and claimed the land for France?
questions.x: Cartier heard the Iroquoian word "kanata," meaning village, and it eventually became the name Canada.

questions.q: Which priest launched the 1810 Mexican War of Independence with the Grito de Dolores?
questions.x: Mexico celebrates the cry on September 16. Hidalgo was captured and executed in 1811, but the movement carried on.

questions.q: Who declared Brazil independent from Portugal in 1822?
questions.x: Pedro was the son of Portugal's king, and he became Brazil's first emperor after declaring independence with the cry "Independence or death!"

questions.q: In which year did Canada become a self-governing dominion through Confederation?
questions.x: The new country began with four provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. July 1 is now Canada Day.

questions.q: In which year did the Australian colonies federate into the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.x: Federation came on January 1, 1901. Canberra, chosen as a compromise capital between Sydney and Melbourne, was founded in 1913.

questions.q: Which country became the first self-governing nation to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
questions.x: Suffragist Kate Sheppard led the campaign, and her petition had nearly 32,000 signatures. She appears on New Zealand's 10-dollar note.

questions.q: Which Russian tsar freed the serfs in 1861?
questions.x: Known as the "Tsar Liberator," Alexander II freed an estimated 23 million serfs. He was assassinated in 1881.

questions.q: Who founded the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan in 1603?
questions.x: His family ruled Japan in relative peace for over 250 years, until the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

questions.q: Which Korean admiral used armored "turtle ships" against Japanese invasions in the 1590s?
questions.x: Yi won all of his major naval battles, and his statue stands in the center of Seoul today.

questions.q: Which Korean king oversaw the creation of the Hangul alphabet in 1443?
questions.x: Hangul was designed so that ordinary people could learn it quickly. Korea celebrates it with a national holiday.

questions.q: What was Genghis Khan's birth name?
questions.x: He was given the title Genghis Khan, roughly "universal ruler," at a gathering of Mongol tribes in 1206.

questions.q: Which dynasty's forces defeated the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
questions.x: It was among the first major defeats of the Mongol army and halted their advance toward Egypt.

questions.q: Which short-lived Chinese dynasty, from 581 to 618, linked rivers by building the Grand Canal?
questions.x: The Grand Canal grew to be the longest artificial waterway in the world and carried grain from the south to the north for centuries.

questions.q: Who was the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right?
questions.x: She ruled from 690 to 705 during the Tang era and founded her own short dynasty, the Zhou.

questions.q: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
questions.x: The VOC is often called the first publicly traded company, and at its peak it was among the richest companies in history.

questions.q: Who invented dynamite in 1867?
questions.x: Nobel's will left his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes. A newspaper's mistaken obituary for him reportedly influenced the decision.

questions.q: Which 1783 treaty formally ended the American Revolutionary War?
questions.x: Britain recognized American independence and agreed to borders reaching west to the Mississippi River.

questions.q: Who was the first monarch of England's Tudor dynasty?
questions.x: Henry VII won the crown at Bosworth in 1485 and strengthened royal finances. He united the houses of Lancaster and York by marrying Elizabeth of York.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor began building a wall across northern Britain in AD 122?
questions.x: The wall ran about 73 miles coast to coast. Antoninus Pius later built another, the Antonine Wall, further north in Scotland.

questions.q: Which Aztec ruler was emperor when Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519?
questions.x: Moctezuma welcomed the Spaniards into Tenochtitlan, and he died in 1520. Cuauhtemoc, his successor's successor, led the last defense.

questions.q: Which Greek writer is often called the "Father of History"?
questions.x: His Histories, about the Greco-Persian Wars, mix careful inquiry with colorful stories, and the Greek word historia means "inquiry."
